title: Dauphiné
capsule: Dauphiné was a feudal principality in the southeastern French Alps, centred on Grenoble, whose rulers bore the distinctive title Dauphin from the mid-thirteenth century — a sobriquet derived from the personal device of the Guigues comital dynasty. At its height under Dauphin Humbert II (r. 1333–1349) the territory stretched from the Rhône valley to the alpine passes above Briançon and Embrun. Facing bankruptcy and without heirs, Humbert II transferred Dauphiné to the French crown by the Act of Romans (30 March 1349), establishing the custom that the French heir-apparent henceforth bore the title Dauphin de France. The region retained its own parlement and fiscal institutions until the Revolution abolished provincial privileges in 1790.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The principality's boundaries are reasonably well attested through medieval charters and the 1349 cession document, though exact border alignments with Savoy and Provence shifted across the medieval period.
